[p. 13] The literal meaning of *al-Fatihah* (the Opener) is that which is first in what it is meant to be begun with. It was then applied to the first part of anything, such as speech. The *ta'* (ة) in the word marks the transfer from an adjective to a noun. This surah was therefore named *Fatihat al-Kitab* (the Opener of the Book), because the Book is opened with it. It is the first thing a scribe writes from the Mushaf (the codex), and the first thing a reciter recites from the Noble Book, even though it was not the first part of the Qur'an to be revealed.

This noble surah became known by this name during the lifetime of the Prophet.

It has been said that it is Meccan, and it has been said that it is Medinan.

Al-Wahidi, in *Asbab al-Nuzul* (Occasions of Revelation), and al-Tha'labi, in his *Tafsir*, reported from Ali, may God be pleased with him, that he said: "*Fatihat al-Kitab* was revealed in Mecca, from a treasure beneath the Throne."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, in *al-Musannaf*, and Abu Nu'aym and al-Bayhaqi, both in *Dala'il al-Nubuwwah* (Proofs of Prophethood), and al-Tha'labi and al-Wahidi, related through the chain of 'Umar ibn Shurahbil that "when the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, complained to Khadijah about what he experienced at the beginning of the revelation, she took him to Waraqah, and he informed him. Waraqah said to him: 'When I am alone, I hear a call behind me: "O Muhammad! O Muhammad! O Muhammad!" and I run off into the earth.' He said: 'Do not do that. When it comes to you, stand firm until you hear what it says, then come to me and inform me.' When he was alone, it called him: 'O Muhammad, say: ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾,' until it reached ﴿nor of those who are astray﴾." This is the hadith.

Abu Nu'aym reported in *al-Dala'il* from a man of the Banu Salamah: "When the youths of the Banu Salamah embraced Islam, and the son of 'Amr ibn al-Jamuh embraced Islam, the wife of 'Amr said to him: 'Would you like to hear from your father what is related from him?' He asked him, and he recited to him: (﴿All praise is due to God, Lord of the worlds﴾), and that was before the Hijrah."

Abu Bakr ibn al-Anbari, in *al-Masahif* (The Codices), reported from 'Ubadah that he said: "*Fatihat al-Kitab* was revealed in Mecca."

This is the sum of what those who said it was revealed in Mecca cited as evidence.

Those who said it was revealed in Medina cited what Ibn Abi Shaybah in *al-Musannaf*, Abu Sa'id ibn al-A'rabi in his *Mu'jam*, and al-Tabarani in *al-Awsat* reported through the chain of Mujahid ibn Abi Hurayrah: "Iblis wailed when *Fatihat al-Kitab* was revealed," and it was revealed in Medina.

Ibn Abi Shaybah in *al-Musannaf*, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Abu Nu'aym in *al-Hilyah*, and others reported through various chains from Mujahid, who said: "*Fatihat al-Kitab* was revealed in Medina." It has also been said that it was revealed twice, once in Mecca and once in Medina, in order to reconcile these reports.

* *

It is also called *Umm al-Kitab* (the Mother of the Book). Al-Bukhari said at the beginning of the *Tafsir* chapter: "It was called *Umm al-Kitab* because the writing of it in the codices begins with it, and the recitation of it in prayer begins with it."

Ibn al-Durays, in *Fada'il al-Qur'an* (Virtues of the Qur'an), reported from Ayyub, from Muhammad ibn Sirin, that he disliked saying "*Umm al-Kitab*" and said: "God the Exalted said: ﴿And with Him is the Mother of the Book﴾ [al-Ra'd 13:39]. Rather, one should say *Fatihat al-Kitab*."

It is called *al-Fatihah* because the recitation is opened with it, and the Companions began the writing of the Imam Mushaf (the standard codex) with it.

Ibn Kathir said in his *Tafsir*: "Its being called *al-Sab' al-Mathani* (the Seven Oft-Repeated) is established. They said: this is because it is repeated in prayer, for it is recited in every rak'ah."

Ahmad reported from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, who said of *Umm al-Qur'an* (the Mother of the Qur'an): "It is the Mother of the Qur'an, it is the Seven Oft-Repeated, and it is the Great Qur'an."

Ibn Jarir reported in his *Tafsir* from Abu Hurayrah, from the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, who said: "It is the Mother of the Qur'an, it is *Fatihat al-Kitab*, and it is the Seven Oft-Repeated."

Ibn Mardawayh reported something similar in his *Tafsir*, and al-Daraqutni from his hadith, and he said: "They are all trustworthy."

Al-Bayhaqi related from Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, and Abu Hurayrah that they interpreted the words of God the Exalted, ﴿seven of the oft-repeated﴾ [al-Hijr 15:87], as referring to *al-Fatihah*.

Among its names, as recorded by al-Zamakhshari in *al-Kashshaf*, are: *Surat al-Kanz* (the Surah of the Treasure), *al-Wafiyah* (the Sufficient), *Surat al-Hamd* (the Surah of Praise), and *Surat al-Salah* (the Surah of Prayer).

Al-Tha'labi reported that Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah used to call *Fatihat al-Kitab* *al-Waqiyah* (the Protector).

Al-Tha'labi also reported from 'Abd Allah ibn Yahya ibn Abi Kathir that a questioner asked him about reciting *al-Fatihah* behind the Imam. He said: "Are you asking about *al-Kafiyah* (the Sufficient)?" The questioner said: "And what is *al-Kafiyah*?" He said: "*al-Fatihah*. Do you not know that it suffices in place of others, and nothing else suffices in its place?"

He also reported from al-Sha'bi that a man complained to him of a pain in the side, and he said: "Take to the foundation of the Qur'an." He asked: "And what is the foundation of the Qur'an?" He said: "*Fatihat al-Kitab*."

Al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* reported from Anas, from the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, who said: "God has given me, among what He has bestowed upon me, *Fatihat al-Kitab*, and He said: 'It is from the treasures of My Throne.'" Ishaq ibn Rahawayh in his *Musnad* reported something similar from Ali, as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet) report.

Al-Daraqutni, in his *Tafsir* of *al-Fatihah*, mentioned twelve names for it. It consists of seven verses without disagreement, as Ibn Kathir related.

Al-Qurtubi said: "The Community is unanimous that *Fatihat al-Kitab* consists of seven verses, except for what is related from Husayn al-Ju'fi that it has six, and that is an anomalous view. And except for what is related from 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd that he made ﴿You alone we worship﴾ a separate verse, so that according to him it has eight; this too is anomalous." End of quote.

They differed only about the *basmalah* (﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾), as will come, God willing.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Muhammad ibn Nasr in *Kitab al-Salah* (The Book of Prayer), and Ibn al-Anbari in *al-Masahif*, reported from Muhammad ibn Sirin that Ubayy ibn Ka'b and 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, may God be pleased with them, used to write *Fatihat al-Kitab* and the two *Mu'awwidhatayn* (the two Surahs of Seeking Refuge), while Ibn Mas'ud wrote none of them.

'Abd ibn Humayd reported from Ibrahim that 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, may God be pleased with him, did not write *Fatihat al-Kitab* in the Mushaf, and he said: "If I had written it, I would have written it at the beginning of everything."

Hadiths have been related about the virtue of this surah. Among them is what al-Bukhari, Ahmad, Abu Dawud, and al-Nasa'i reported from the hadith of Abu Sa'id ibn al-Mu'alla, that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, said to him: "I will certainly teach you the greatest surah in the Qur'an before you leave the mosque." He said: "He took my hand, and when he wanted to leave the mosque I said: 'O Messenger of God, you said you would teach me the greatest surah in the Qur'an?' He said: 'Yes: ﴿All praise is due to God, Lord of the worlds﴾. It is the Seven Oft-Repeated and the Great Qur'an which I have been given.'"

Ahmad and al-Tirmidhi, who authenticated it, reported from the hadith of Ubayy ibn Ka'b that the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, said to him: "Would you like me to teach you a surah that has not been revealed in the Torah, nor in the Gospel, nor in the Psalms, nor in the Furqan (the Criterion) like it?" Then he informed him that it was *al-Fatihah*.

Al-Nasa'i also reported it. Ahmad in *al-Musnad* reported from the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn Jabir that "the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, said to him: 'Shall I not inform you of the best surah in the Qur'an?' I said: 'Yes, O Messenger of God.' He said: 'Recite ﴿All praise is due to God, Lord of the worlds﴾ until you finish it.'"

[p. 14] In its chain is Ibn 'Aqil, and major imams have relied upon him as evidence, and the rest of its narrators are trustworthy.

This 'Abd Allah ibn Jabir is al-'Abdi, as Ibn al-Jawzi said. It has also been said that he is al-Ansari al-Bayadi, as Ibn 'Asakir said.

In the two *Sahihs* (Bukhari and Muslim) and other collections, from the hadith of Abu Sa'id: "The Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, said, when they informed him that a man had treated a scorpion-stung person with *Fatihat al-Kitab*: 'How did he know that it is a remedy?'" This is the hadith.

Muslim in his *Sahih*, and al-Nasa'i in his *Sunan*, reported from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "While the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, was with Jibril, he heard a creaking above him. Jibril raised his eyes to the sky and said: 'This is a gate that has been opened in the sky, which has never been opened before.' Then an angel descended from it and came to the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, and said: 'Rejoice in two lights that have been given to you, which no prophet before you has been given: *Fatihat al-Kitab* and the closing verses of Surat al-Baqarah. You will not recite a letter of them except that you will be given it.'"

Muslim, al-Nasa'i, and al-Tirmidhi, who authenticated it, reported from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah: "Whoever performs a prayer in which he does not recite *Umm al-Qur'an* (the Mother of the Qur'an), it is *khidaj* (deficient) — three times — not complete."

Al-Bazzar in his *Musnad*, through a weak chain, reported from Anas that "the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, said: 'When you lay your side on the bed and recite *Fatihat al-Kitab* and say ﴿He is God, One﴾ [al-Ikhlas 112:1], you will be safe from everything except death.'"

Al-Tabarani in *al-Awsat*, through a weak chain, reported from Abu Zayd, who had companionship with the Prophet, who said: "I was with the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, on one of the roads of Medina, and he heard a man performing the night prayer and reciting *Umm al-Qur'an*. The Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, stood and listened until he finished it, then said: 'There is nothing in the Qur'an like it.'"

Sa'id ibn Mansur in his *Sunan*, and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman*, reported from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, said: "*Fatihat al-Kitab* is a cure from every ailment."

Abu al-Shaykh reported something similar from his hadith and from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, as a marfu' report.

Al-Darimi and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman*, through a chain whose narrators are trustworthy, reported from 'Abd al-Malik ibn 'Umayr that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, said concerning *Fatihat al-Kitab*: "A cure from every disease."

Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, Ibn al-Sunni in *'Amal al-Yawm wa al-Laylah* (The Practice of the Day and Night), Ibn Jarir, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, reported from Kharijah ibn al-Salt al-Tamimi, from his paternal uncle, that he "came to the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, then turned back from his presence, and passed by a people among whom was a man who was insane and bound with iron. His people said: 'Do you have anything with which to treat this one? Indeed, your companion has come with good.' He said: 'So I recited *Fatihat al-Kitab* over him for three days, twice each day, morning and evening, gathering my saliva and then spitting, and he was cured. They gave me a hundred sheep, so I came to the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, and mentioned that to him. He said: "Eat. Whoever eats by an invalid incantation has eaten by a valid incantation."'"

Al-Firyabi in his *Tafsir* reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "*Fatihat al-Kitab* is a third of the Qur'an."

Al-Tabarani in *al-Awsat*, through a weak chain, reported from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "The Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, said: 'Whoever recites *Umm al-Qur'an* and ﴿He is God, One﴾, it is as if he has recited a third of the Qur'an.'" 'Abd ibn Humayd in his *Musnad*, through a weak chain, reported from Ibn 'Abbas, traced to the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace: "*Fatihat al-Kitab* equals two-thirds of the Qur'an."

Al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Abu Dhar al-Harawi in *Fada'ilihi* (its virtues), and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* reported from Anas that "the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, was on a journey. He dismounted, and a man from among his companions walked up beside him. The Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, turned to him and said: 'Shall I not inform you of the best of the Qur'an?' Then he recited to him: ﴿All praise is due to God, Lord of the worlds﴾."

Abu Nu'aym and al-Daylami reported from Abu al-Darda', who said: "The Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, said: '*Fatihat al-Kitab* repays what no other part of the Qur'an repays. Even if *Fatihat al-Kitab* were placed in one pan of the scale, and the Qur'an in the other pan, *Fatihat al-Kitab* would outweigh the Qur'an seven times.'"

Abu 'Ubayd in *Fada'il al-Qur'an*, from al-Hasan as a mursal report (one whose chain omits the Companion), said: "The Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, said: 'Whoever recites *Fatihat al-Kitab* has recited as if he had recited the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, and the Furqan.'"

* *

The commentators differed over whether the basmalah (the phrase "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful") is an independent verse at the beginning of every surah that is written at its start, or part of a verse at the beginning of every surah, or a verse only in al-Fatihah and not in the others, or not a verse at all in any surah but written only as a separator (*fasl*). The positions and their evidences are set out at length in the place where that subject is discussed.

They agreed that it is part of a verse in Surah an-Naml, where Allah says: ﴿Indeed, it is from Solomon, and indeed it is: "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful"﴾ [an-Naml: 30].

The readers (*qurra'*) of Makkah and Kufah were firm that it is a verse of al-Fatihah and of every surah. The readers of Madinah, Basrah and Syria disagreed with them. They did not count it as a verse, either of al-Fatihah or of any other surah. They said that it was written only as a separator and for blessing (*tabarruk*).

Abu Dawud related with a sound chain (*isnad*) from Ibn 'Abbas that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not know the separation between surahs until there was revealed to him: ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾." Al-Hakim also related it in *al-Mustadrak*.

Ibn Khuzaymah related in his *Sahih* from Umm Salamah that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited the basmalah at the beginning of al-Fatihah in the prayer and otherwise, as a verse." In its chain is 'Amr ibn Harun al-Balkhi, in whom there is weakness. Ad-Daraqutni related something similar, marfu' (traced to the Prophet), from Abu Hurayrah.

Just as there was disagreement over its being a verse, there was disagreement over reciting it aloud (*al-jahr*) in the prayer.

An-Nasa'i in his *Sunan*, and Ibn Khuzaymah and Ibn Hibban in their two *Sahih*s, and al-Hakim in *al-Mustadrak* related from Abu Hurayrah that "he prayed and recited the basmalah aloud in his recitation, and said after he had finished: 'I am indeed the most similar of you to the prayer of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).'" Ad-Daraqutni, al-Khatib, al-Bayhaqi and others authenticated it.

Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi related from Ibn 'Abbas: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to open the prayer with: ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾." At-Tirmidhi said: "Its chain is not of that standard." Al-Hakim also related it from Ibn 'Abbas with the wording: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to recite aloud ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾," and then said: "It is sound."

Al-Bukhari in his *Sahih* related from Anas that he was asked about the recitation of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: "His recitation was elongated (*madd*). Then he recited ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾, elongating 'In the name of Allah,' elongating '(the Most) Gracious,' and elongating '(the Most) Merciful'."

Ahmad in *al-Musnad*, Abu Dawud in *as-Sunan*, Ibn Khuzaymah in his *Sahih*, and al-Hakim in his *Mustadrak* related from Umm Salamah that she said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to pause in his recitation: ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾, ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾, ﴿The Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾, ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾." Ad-Daraqutni said: "Its chain is sound."

Those who held that the basmalah is not recited aloud in the prayer argued with what is in *Sahih Muslim* from 'A'ishah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to open the prayer with the takbir, and the recitation with ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾." In the two *Sahih*s from Anas, who said: "I prayed behind the Prophet (ﷺ), Abu Bakr, 'Umar and 'Uthman, and they used to open with ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾." And in Muslim's wording: "They did not mention ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ at the beginning of the recitation or at its end." The compilers of the *Sunan* related something similar from 'Abdullah ibn Mughaffal.

To this view went the four rightly-guided caliphs (*al-Khulafa' al-Arba'ah*) and a group of the Companions.

Although the hadiths of omission (*tark*) are more authentic, affirmation is more preponderant, since it comes from a sound source. Therefore acting upon it is better, especially since the omission can be interpreted. This requires affirming the basmalah in itself, meaning that it is Qur'an, and affirming it as an attribute (*wasf*), meaning that it is recited aloud when the surah it opens is recited aloud in the prayer.

The full investigation, its refutations, rebuttals and defenses, and the transmission and understanding of the evidences belong to another place.

The object of the preposition *bi* (in) is omitted, and it is either "I recite" (*aqra'*) or "I recite/recount" (*atlu*), because this fits what the basmalah was made the beginning of. Whoever estimates it as preceding (i.e., "I begin with the name of Allah") intends by placing it first to indicate concern with the matter of the verb. Whoever estimates it as following intends by placing it later to indicate restriction (*ikhtisas*), together with the attention given to the name and the indication that beginning with it is more important, since the blessing is obtained through it. By this, the preference for estimating the verb as later in such a context becomes clear. The words of Allah, the Exalted, do not contradict this: ﴿Recite in the name of your Lord who created﴾ [al-'Alaq: 1], because that context is the context of recitation, so commanding it was more important. As for the disagreement among the grammarians (*a'immat an-nahw*) over whether the omitted element is a noun or a verb, little benefit depends upon it.

The *ba'* is for seeking help (*isti'anah*) or for accompaniment (*musahabah*), and az-Zamakhshari preferred the second.

*Ism* (name) is originally *sumw*, whose final radical was dropped. Since it is among the nouns whose initial letters they made quiescent (*sukun*), they added a hamzah at its beginning when they pronounced it, lest the utterance begin with a quiescent letter. It is the word that indicates the named thing (*musamma*). Whoever claims that the name is the named thing, as Abu 'Ubaydah, Sibawayh, al-Baqillani and Ibn Furak said, and as ar-Razi related from the Hashwiyyah, the Karramiyyah and the Ash'ariyyah, has erred a clear error and brought what cannot be understood. There is no evidence requiring contradiction of reason, neither from the Book, nor from the Sunnah, nor from the language of the Arabs. Rather, it is necessary knowledge that the name, which is discrete sounds and composed letters, is other than the named thing, which is its referent. The discussion is elaborated in the science of kalam (theology).

It is established in the two *Sahih*s from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah: "Indeed Allah has ninety-nine names; whoever counts them enters Paradise." Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And to Allah belong the most beautiful names, so call upon Him by them﴾ [al-A'raf: 180], and He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Say: Call upon Allah or call upon the Most Gracious; whichever you call upon, to Him belong the most beautiful names﴾ [al-Isra': 110].

*Allah* is a proper name for the Essence that necessarily exists (*dhat al-wajib al-wujud*), which is not applied to anything else. Its origin is *Ilah*, the hamzah was dropped and the definite article was substituted for it, so it became obligatory.

Before the deletion, it was among the common nouns (*asma' al-ajnas*) which applied to every worshipped thing, whether by truth or falsehood. Then it came to be dominant for what is worshipped in truth, like "the Star" (*an-najm*) and "the Thunderbolt" (*as-sa'q*). So before the deletion it was among the dominant designations (*a'lam al-ghalibah*), and after it, among the specific proper names (*a'lam al-mukhtassah*).

*Ar-Rahman* and *ar-Rahim* are two names derived from *ar-rahmah* (mercy) in the form of intensification (*mubalaghah*), and *Rahman* is more intensive than *Rahim*.

The words of Ibn Jarir indicate the reporting of consensus on this. For this reason they said: "Rahman of this world and the Hereafter, and Rahim of this world." It is established that an increase in the form indicates an increase in meaning.

Ibn al-Anbari and az-Zajjaj said: "Ar-Rahman is Hebrew, and ar-Rahim is Arabic." Others disagreed with the two of them.

*Ar-Rahman* is among the dominant attributes; it has not been used for anyone other than Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

As for the saying of Banu Hanifah about Musaylimah, "Rahman of Yamamah," az-Zamakhshari said in *al-Kashshaf* that it is a form of their obstinacy in their disbelief.

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: "Ar-Rahman is a general name encompassing all kinds of mercy, and it is exclusive to Allah, the Exalted. Ar-Rahim pertains only to the direction of the believers." Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And He is ever Merciful to the believers﴾ [al-Ahzab: 43].

Hadiths have been related concerning its virtue. Among them is what Sa'id ibn Mansur related in his *Sunan*, and Ibn Khuzaymah in his *Kitab al-Basmalah*, and al-Bayhaqi, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Shaytan stole from the people the greatest verse of the Qur'an: ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾."

Ad-Daraqutni related with a weak chain from Ibn 'Umar that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When Jibril came to me with the revelation, the first thing he would convey to me was: ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾."

Ibn Abi Hatim in his *Tafsir*, and al-Hakim in *al-Mustadrak*, and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* (which authenticated it), related from Ibn 'Abbas that "'Uthman ibn 'Affan asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾, and he said: 'It is one of the names of Allah, and between it and the Greatest Name of Allah there is only the closeness of the black of the eye to its white.'"

Ibn Jarir, Ibn 'Adi in *al-Kamil*, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym in *al-Hilyah*, Ibn 'Asakir in *Tarikh Dimashq*, and ath-Tha'labi related with an extremely weak chain from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed 'Isa, son of Maryam, his mother enrolled him in the school (*kuttab*) so that he might be taught. The teacher said to him: 'Write: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.' 'Isa said to him: 'And what is "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful"?' The teacher said: 'I do not know.' 'Isa said to him: 'The *ba'* is the splendour (*bahá'*) of Allah, the *sin* is His radiance (*sana*), the *mim* is His kingdom (*mamlakah*), Allah is the God of the gods, ar-Rahman is the Rahman of this world and the Hereafter, and ar-Rahim is the Rahim of the Hereafter.'" In its chain is Isma'il ibn Yahya, who is a liar (*kadhdhab*).

Ibn al-Jawzi included this hadith in *al-Mawdu'at* (the fabricated hadiths).

Ibn Mardawayh and ath-Tha'labi related from Jabir that he said: "When ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ was revealed, the clouds fled to the east, the wind became still, the sea was agitated, the animals pricked up their ears, the devils were pelted from the sky, and Allah swore by His might and majesty that He would not let anything be named upon without blessing it."

Abu Nu'aym and ad-Daylami related from 'A'ishah that she said: "When ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ was revealed, the mountains clamored until the people of Makkah heard their echo. They said: 'Muhammad has bewitched the mountains.' So Allah sent a smoke that overshadowed the people of Makkah. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Whoever recites ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ with certainty, the mountains glorify Allah along with him, though he does not hear that from them.'"

Ad-Daylami related from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾, Allah records for him four thousand good deeds for each letter, erases four thousand evil deeds from him, and raises him four thousand degrees."

It has also been said: the people of every age are an *'alam*. This was said by al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl.

Ibn 'Abbas said: *Al-'Alamun* are the jinn and mankind.

al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubayd said: *al-'Alam* is an expression for what has intellect, and they are four communities: mankind, the jinn, the angels, and the devils.

*Al-'Alam* is not said of animals, because this plural is only the plural of what has intellect.

al-Qurtubi related these sayings in his *Tafsir*, mentioned their evidence, and said: The first of these sayings is the most correct, because it includes every created and existing thing. Its proof is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿قَالَ فِرْعَوْنُ وَمَا رَبُّ الْعَالَمِينَ * قَالَ رَبُّ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ وَمَا بَيْنَهُمَا﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 23–24], "Pharaoh said: 'And what is the Lord of the worlds?' He said: 'The Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them.'" It is derived from knowledge (*'ilm*) and sign (*'alamah*), because it points to its Originator. So said al-Zajjaj.

He also said: *Al-'alam* is everything that Allah created in this world and in the Hereafter.

On this basis, its plural in this particular form, which is specific to rational beings, is a case of giving precedence to rational beings over others (*taghlib*).

In *al-Kashshaf* it is said: That was permitted because of the descriptive sense in it, which is the indication of the meaning of knowledge.

Al-Firyabi, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim (who authenticated it) related the saying of Ibn 'Abbas mentioned above.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related it from Mujahid.

Ibn Jarir related it from Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

Ibn Jubayr and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His saying, exalted is He: ﴿رَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ﴾, that he said: "The God of all creation: all the heavens and whoever is in them, and all the earths and whoever is in them, and whatever is between them, of what is known and of what is not known."

\* \*

﴿الرَّحْمَنِ الرَّحِيمِ﴾. Their explanation has already been given.

al-Qurtubi said: After *Rabb al-'alamin*, He described Himself, exalted is He, as *al-Rahman al-Rahim*. Because in His attribute of *Rabb al-'alamin* there is an element of inspiring awe (*tarhib*), He joined it with *al-Rahman al-Rahim*, which contains encouragement (*targhib*), so that in His attributes He combines awe of Him with desire for Him. Thus one will be more helpful toward His obedience and more restrained, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿نَبِّئْ عِبَادِي أَنِّي أَنَا الْغَفُورُ الرَّحِيمُ * وَأَنَّ عَذَابِي هُوَ الْعَذَابُ الْأَلِيمُ﴾ [al-Hijr: 49–50], "Inform My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful, and that My punishment is the painful punishment." And He said: ﴿غَافِرِ الذَّنْبِ وَقَابِلِ التَّوْبِ شَدِيدِ الْعِقَابِ﴾ [Ghafir: 3], "Forgiver of sin and Acceptor of repentance, Severe in punishment."

In *Sahih Muslim*, from Abu Hurayrah, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If the believer knew what there is with Allah of punishment, none would hope for His Paradise. And if the disbeliever knew what there is with Allah of mercy, none would despair of His Paradise."

And Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Qatadah, regarding His words ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾, that he said: "[It is the praise for] what He has described of His creation." And regarding His words ﴿the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾, he said: "He praised Himself."

Then he mentioned the remainder of al-Fatiha: ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾. It is recited as "Maliki," "Maliki" and "Maliki" with the lam sukun, and as "Malaka" in the verbal form.

The scholars differed over which of the two is more eloquent: "Maliki" (King) or "Maliki" (Master). It was said that "Maliki" (King) is more general and more eloquent than "Maliki" (Master), since every king is a master, but not every master is a king; and because the command of the king takes effect over the master in his possession, so that he cannot act except within the management of the king. This was stated by Abu Ubayd and al-Mubarrad, and al-Zamakhshari preferred it.

It was also said that "Maliki" (Master) is more eloquent, because he is master of the people and others, so the master has greater and more far-reaching authority.

Abu Hatim said: "Maliki" (Master) is more eloquent than "Maliki" (King) in praising the Creator, while "Maliki" (King) is more eloquent in praising created beings than "Maliki" (Master), because a created master may not be a king, and when God Most High is Master, He is King.

Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi chose this view.

The truth is that each of the two attributes has a kind of particularity not found in the other. The master can do with his property what the king cannot, such as selling, giving as a gift, freeing and the like; and the king can do what the master cannot in matters of management, governance, protection and the care of the subjects' interests. Thus the master is stronger than the king in some matters, and the king is stronger than the master in some matters.

As for the difference between the two attributes in relation to the Lord, glorified is He: the King is an attribute of His essence, and the Master is an attribute of His action.

"Day of Judgment" (yawm al-din): the day of recompense from the Lord, glorified is He, to His servants, as He said: ﴿And what will make you know what the Day of Judgment is?﴾ ﴿Then what will make you know what the Day of Judgment is?﴾ ﴿The Day when no soul will have power for another soul at all, and the command that Day is entirely God's﴾ [al-Infitar: 17-19]. This idafa (genitive construction) to a time-noun is by way of extension (ittisa'), like the saying: "O thief, tonight the people of the house!" Although "Day of Judgment" is future, the active participle and what is similar to it may be annexed to a future time, as in your saying: "This is one who strikes Zayd tomorrow."

Al-Tirmidhi narrated from Umm Salama that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to recite "Maliki" without an alif.

Ibn al-Anbari narrated a similar report from Anas.

Ahmad and al-Tirmidhi also narrated from Anas that the Prophet (ﷺ), Abu Bakr, 'Umar and 'Uthman used to recite "Maliki" with an alif.

Sa'id ibn Mansur narrated a similar report from Ibn 'Umar, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Wakee' in his Tafsir, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Abu Dawud also narrated a similar report from al-Zuhri, raising it to the Prophet (ﷺ) as a mursal report.

'Abd al-Razzaq in his Tafsir, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Abu Dawud also narrated it from Ibn al-Musayyib, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) as a mursal report.

This has been related through many routes, so it is preferred over the first.

al-Hakim narrated from Abu Hurayra, and declared it sahih: "That the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to recite ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾." Likewise al-Tabarani in al-Kabir narrated it from Ibn Mas'ud, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Ibn Jarir and al-Hakim, who declared it sahih, narrated from Ibn Mas'ud and a number of the Companions that they interpreted "Day of Judgment" as the Day of Reckoning.

Likewise Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas.

'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatada, who said: "Yawm al-din: the day on which God requites the servants for their deeds."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 1, verse 5:

The reading of the Seven (al-Sab'a) and others is with a shaddah on the ya' (iyyaka, with tashdid on the yā'). 'Amr ibn Fa'id read it with the ya' lightened and with a kasrah. Al-Fadl and al-Raqqashi read it with a fathah on the hamzah (ayyaka... with a fathah on the hamza). Abu al-Sawwar al-Ghanawi read hayyaka in both places, and this is a well-known dialect (lughah).

The detached pronoun is iyya, and what attaches to it of the kaf, the ha' and the ya' are letters that indicate address, absence and speaking (the first person). They have no place in i'rab (grammatical case analysis), as the majority of scholars held. Placing it before the verb is for the purpose of restriction (ikhtisas); it is said also that it is for emphasis (ihtimam). The correct view is that it serves both purposes, and there is no conflict between the implications.

The meaning: we single You out for worship, and we single You out for seeking help; we do not worship other than You, nor seek help from other than You. Worship ('ibadah) is the utmost extent of submission and humility.

Ibn Kathir said: In the Shariah, it is an expression for what combines the perfection of love, submission and fear.

He shifted from the third person (absence) to the second person (address) for the purpose of iltifat (shift of grammatical person), because when speech is moved from one style to another, it is more pleasing to refresh the listener's energy and more effective in waking him, as established in the science of ma'ani (rhetoric).

The use of the nun in the two verbs (na'budu and nasta'in) is for the purpose of the reciter speaking about himself and about his kind of servants. It is said that since the station is great, one individual cannot bear it alone, considering himself small and belittling himself; so the use of the nun is for the purpose of humility, not for the glorification of the self. Worship was placed before seeking help because the first is a means to the second, and placing means before the goal is a cause of attaining the aims. The unrestricted "seeking help" is for the purpose of generality.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding his saying "Iyyaka na'budu": he means, "Iyyaka nuwahhid wa nakhaf ya Rabbana, la ghayrak" (We affirm Your oneness and fear You alone, O our Lord, not other than You), and "Iyyaka nasta'in" (we seek Your help in obedience to You and in all our affairs).

Ibn Kathir related from Qatadah that he said regarding "Iyyaka na'budu wa iyyaka nasta'in": He commands you to devote worship to Him sincerely, and to seek His help in your affairs.

In Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of al-Ala' ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, from his father, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: Allah the Exalted says: "I have divided the prayer between Myself and My servant into two halves; half of it is for Me and half of it is for My servant, and My servant shall have what he asks." When the servant says "Al-hamdu lillahi Rabbi al-'alamin," He says: "My servant has praised Me." When he says "Al-Rahmani al-Rahim," He says: "My servant has extolled Me." When he says "Maliki yawmi al-din," He says: "My servant has glorified Me." When he says "Iyyaka na'budu wa iyyaka nasta'in," He says: "This is between Me and My servant, and My servant shall have what he asks." When he says "Ihdina al-sirat al-mustaqim, sirat alladhina an'amta 'alayhim, ghayr al-maghdubi 'alayhim wa la al-dallin," He says: "This is for My servant, and My servant shall have what he asks."

Abu al-Qasim al-Baghawi and al-Bawardi together in Ma'rifat al-Sahabah, al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, and Abu Nu'aym in al-Dala'il, related from Anas ibn Malik, from Abu Talhah, who said: "We were with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in a battle, and he met the enemy, and I heard him say: 'Ya Malika yawmi al-din, iyyaka na'budu wa iyyaka nasta'in.' He said: I saw men being struck down, and the angels striking them from in front of them and from behind them."

The majority of readers recited it with the letter ṣād (ṣirāṭ). It was also recited as *al-sirāṭ* with sīn and *al-zirāṭ* with zāy. Guidance (*hidāyah*) may sometimes have its verb used without a preposition, as here, and as in His saying ﴿And We guided him to the two highways﴾ [al-Balad: 10]. It may also take *ilā* (to), as in His saying ﴿He chose him and guided him to a straight path﴾ [al-Nahl: 121], ﴿So guide them to the path of Hellfire﴾ [al-Saffat: 23], and ﴿And indeed you guide to a straight path﴾ [al-Shura: 52]. It may take *al-lām* (to/for), as in His saying ﴿Praise be to God who guided us to this﴾ [al-A'raf: 43], and ﴿Indeed this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright﴾ [al-Isra': 9]. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Its original usage is to take *al-lām* or *ilā*. End of quotation."

It means guidance (*al-irshād*), or success (*al-tawfīq*), or inspiration (*al-ilhām*), or indication (*al-dalālah*).

Many of the later scholars distinguished between the meaning of the form that takes its object directly and the form that does not. They said: the meaning of the first is indication (*al-dalālah*), and the meaning of the second is bringing to (*al-īṣāl*).

When guidance is requested by one who is already guided, its meaning is a request for increase, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance﴾ [Muhammad: 17], and ﴿And those who strive for Us, We will surely guide them to Our paths﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 69].

The *ṣirāṭ* is the road. Ibn Jarir said: "The community of the people of interpretation (*ta'wīl*) all agree that the straight path (*al-ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm*) is the clear road that has no crookedness in it, and it is so in the language of all the Arabs."

He said: "Then the Arabs use the *ṣirāṭ* metaphorically, and they describe the straight by its straightness and the crooked by its crookedness."

Al-Hakim narrated it and graded it as sound, and al-Dhahabi criticised him for this, from Abu Hurayrah: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ with the letter ṣād."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd and al-Bukhari in his *Tarikh* narrated from Ibn Abbas that "he recited *al-ṣirāṭ* with the letter sīn."

Ibn al-Anbari narrated from Ibn Kathir that he used to recite *al-sirāṭ* with sīn.

He also narrated from Hamza that he used to recite *al-zirāṭ* with zāy. Al-Farra' said: "It is a dialect of 'Udhrah, Kalb and Banu al-Qayn."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ means: "Inspire us with Your true religion."

Ibn Jarir narrated something similar from him, as did Ibn al-Mundhir.

Waki', Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Hakim (who graded it as sound) narrated from Jabir ibn Abd Allah that he said: "It is the religion of Islam, and it is wider than what lies between the heaven and the earth."

Ibn Jarir narrated something similar from Ibn Abbas.

He also narrated something similar from Ibn Mas'ud and a number of the Companions.

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it as good), al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Hakim (who graded it as sound), Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* narrated from al-Nawwas ibn Sam'an, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who said: "God has struck a parable: a straight path, and on either side of the path are two walls in which there are open doors, and over the doors are lowered curtains. At the entrance of the path there is a caller saying: 'O people, enter the path all together and do not scatter.' And there is a caller calling from above the path. When a person wants to open any of those doors, he says: 'Woe to you! Do not open it, for if you open it, you will enter it.' So the path is Islam, the two walls are the limits of God, the open doors are the forbidden things of God, that caller at the head of the path is the Book of God, and the caller from above is God's admonisher in the heart of every believer."

Ibn Kathir said after narrating it: "It is a good and sound chain."

Waki', Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Abu Bakr al-Anbari, al-Hakim (who graded it as sound) and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "It is the Book of God."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Adi and Ibn Asakir narrated from Abu al-'Aliyah, who said: "It is the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and his two companions after him."

Al-Hakim narrated, and graded as sound, something similar from Abu al-'Aliyah, from Ibn Abbas.

Al-Qurtubi narrated from al-Fudayl ibn Iyad that he said: "The straight path is the road of the Pilgrimage." He said: "This is particular, and the general meaning is more appropriate." End of quotation.

Everything that has been narrated in the interpretation of this verse, other than this report from al-Fudayl, confirms one another, for whoever follows Islam, or the Qur'an, or the Prophet, has indeed followed the truth.

Ibn Jarir mentioned something similar to this, saying: "What is most appropriate to the interpretation of this verse, in my view, is what is meant by it: 'Grant us steadfastness in what You have approved, and grant success in it to those of Your servants upon whom You have bestowed favour, in word and in deed.' That is the straight path, because whoever is granted success in it from among those upon whom God has bestowed favour, from among the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous, has been granted success in Islam, in confirming the messengers, in holding fast to the Book, in acting on what God has commanded him, in refraining from what He has forbidden him, in following the method of the Prophet (ﷺ) and the method of the four Caliphs and of every righteous servant. All of that is part of the straight path." End of quotation.

Shawkani's commentary (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 1, verse 7:

The word ﴿ṣirāṭa﴾ is in the accusative because it is a substitute (badal) for the first word, and its purpose is emphasis (tawkīd), given the repetition and reiteration it contains. It is also permissible for it to be an explanatory apposition (ʿaṭf bayān), whose purpose is clarification.

Those upon whom God has bestowed His favour are those mentioned in Surah al-Nisa', where He says: ﴿And whoever obeys God and the Messenger - those are with the ones upon whom God has bestowed favour: of the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous. And excellent are those as companions.﴾ ﴿That is the bounty from God, and sufficient is God as Knower.﴾ [al-Nisa': 69-70]. He used the general term "favour" to encompass every kind of favour.

﴿Not of those who have evoked anger﴾ is a substitute for ﴿those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾, in the sense that they combined two blessings: the blessing of faith and safety from that (anger). It is valid to make ﴿ghayr﴾ a qualifier of a definite noun, even though ghayr is not made definite by being annexed to definite nouns, because the indefiniteness in it is not present here, since the difference between the two categories is well known.

As for al-ghaḍab (anger) in the language, al-Qurtubi said: it is intensity; a man who is ghaḍūb is one of harsh disposition; and al-ghaḍūb is a wicked snake because of its ferocity.

He said: the meaning of anger when applied to God is the will to punish; so it is an attribute of His essence, or it is the punishment itself; and from it is the hadith: "Indeed charity extinguishes the anger of the Lord," so it is an attribute of His act.

In al-Kashshaf it is said: it is the will to take vengeance upon the disobedient and to inflict punishment upon them, and to do to them what a king does when he becomes angry with those under his authority. The difference between the first ʿalayhim and the second ʿalayhim is that the first is in the place of an accusative as object, and the second is in the place of a nominative as deputy of the subject.

The "lā" in His saying ﴿nor of those who are astray﴾ is an emphasis of the negation implied by (ghayr). Al-ḍalāl in the language of the Arabs, al-Qurtubi said, is departing from the course of moderation and the path of truth; from it comes "ḍalla al-laban fi al-ma'" (the milk was lost in the water), i.e., it disappeared; and from it is His saying ﴿When we are lost in the earth?﴾ [al-Sajdah: 10], i.e., we are hidden by death and become dust.

Wakī', Abū Saʿīd, Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb that he used to recite: "Ṣirāṭa man anʿamta ʿalayhim ghayri al-maghḍūbi ʿalayhim wa ghayri al-ṣāliḥīn." Abū ʿUbayd and ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd narrated that ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr recited likewise.

Al-Anbari narrated from al-Hasan that he used to recite ʿalayhimi with a kasra on the hā' and the mīm and the affirmation of the yā'.

Ibn al-Anbari narrated from al-Aʿraj that he used to recite "ʿalayhumu" with a ḍamma on the hā' and the mīm and the addition of the wāw.

He also narrated from Ibn Kathīr that he used to recite "ʿalayhimu" with a kasra on the hā' and a ḍamma on the mīm with the addition of the wāw.

He also narrated from Abū Isḥāq that he recited ʿalayhim with a ḍamma on the hā' and the mīm without the addition of the wāw.

Ibn Abī Dāwūd narrated from ʿIkrimah and al-Aswad that they both recited like the earlier recitation of ʿUmar.

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His saying ﴿the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾: it says: the way of those upon whom You have bestowed favour from the angels, the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous, who obeyed You and worshipped You. Ibn Jarīr narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās that they are the believers.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd narrated from al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, regarding His saying ﴿the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾: he said, "the prophets."

﴿Not of those who have evoked anger﴾: he said, "the Jews."

﴿Nor of those who are astray﴾: he said, "the Christians."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd narrated the like of this from Mujāhid. He also narrated the like of it from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr.

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Aḥmad in his Musnad, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abū al-Shaykh narrated from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Shaqīq who said: "Someone informed me who heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) while he was at Wadi al-Qura on his horse, and a man from Banu al-Qayn asked him: 'Who are those who have evoked anger, O Messenger of God?' He said: 'The Jews.' He said: 'Then who are those who are astray?' He said: 'The Christians.'"

Ibn Mardawayh narrated it from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Shaqīq from Abū Dharr who said: "I asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ)" and he mentioned it.

Wakī', ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Jarīr narrated it from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Shaqīq who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was besieging the people of Wadi al-Qura, and a man said to him..." to the end, and he did not mention in it "someone informed me who heard the Prophet," as in the first narration.

Al-Bayhaqi narrated it in al-Shuʿab from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Shaqīq, from a man of Banu al-Qayn, from a cousin of his who said: "I came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ)" and he mentioned it.

Sufyan ibn ʿUyaynah narrated it in his Tafsir, and Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr narrated from Ismaʿil ibn Abi Khalid that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Those who have evoked anger are the Jews, and those who are astray are the Christians."

Aḥmad, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it as ḥasan, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Ḥātim and Ibn Ḥibban in his Ṣaḥīḥ narrated from ʿAdi ibn Ḥatim who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Indeed those who have evoked anger are the Jews, and indeed those who are astray are the Christians."

Aḥmad, Abū Dawud, Ibn Ḥibban, al-Ḥakim, who authenticated it, and al-Ṭabarani narrated from al-Sharid who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) passed by me while I was sitting like this, with my left hand placed behind my back, leaning on the palm of my hand, and he said: 'Do you sit the sitting of those who have evoked anger?'" Ibn Kathir said after mentioning the hadith of ʿAdi ibn Ḥatim: This hadith of ʿAdi has been narrated through many chains, and it has many wordings, the mention of which would be lengthy, end of quote.

Adopting this prophetic interpretation is necessary, and it is what the imams of tafsir among the early generations unanimously agreed upon.

Ibn Abi Ḥātim said: I know of no disagreement among the exegetes in interpreting "those who have evoked anger" as the Jews, and "those who are astray" as the Christians.

Verses of the Qur'an bear witness to this prophetic interpretation. God said, addressing the Children of Israel in Surah al-Baqarah: ﴿Wretched is that for which they have sold themselves, that they deny what God has revealed, out of insolence that God should send down His bounty upon whom He wills of His servants. So they have returned with anger upon anger. And for the disbelievers is a humiliating punishment.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 90]

And He said in al-Ma'idah: ﴿Say: Shall I inform you of something worse than that as recompense from God? Those whom God has cursed and upon whom He has become angry and made of them apes and swine and servants of the Taghut. Those are worse in position and further astray from the right way.﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 60]

In the Sirah it is narrated from Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl that when he and a group of his companions went out to Syria seeking the true religion (al-dīn al-ḥanīf), the Jews said to him: "You will not be able to enter with us until you take your share of the anger of God." He said: "I flee from the anger of God." The Christians said to him: "You will not be able to enter with us until you take your share of the wrath of God." He said: "I cannot do that." So he remained upon his natural disposition (fiṭra) and kept away from the worship of idols.

[A benefit concerning the legislation of saying "Amin" after reciting al-Fatihah] Know that the authentic, explicit sunnah, established by continuous transmission (tawātur), has shown this. Among that is what Aḥmad, Abū Dawud and al-Tirmidhi narrated from Wa'il ibn Ḥujr who said: "I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) recite ﴿not of those who have evoked anger, nor of those who are astray﴾ and then say 'Amin,' prolonging his voice with it." In Abū Dawud's version: "He raised his voice with it." Al-Tirmidhi graded it as ḥasan.

Al-Nasa'i, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Majah and al-Ḥakim, who authenticated it, also narrated it, and in one wording of his hadith: that he (ﷺ) said: "My Lord, forgive me. Amin." Al-Ṭabarani and al-Bayhaqi narrated it.

In another wording he said: "Amin" three times. Al-Ṭabarani narrated it.

Wakī' and Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated from Abū Maysarah who said: "When Gabriel recited the Opening of the Book to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), when he reached ﴿nor of those who are astray﴾ he said: 'Say, Amin,' and he said: 'Amin.'"

Ibn Majah narrated from ʿAlī who said: "I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) when he said 'nor of those who are astray,' he said: 'Amin.'"

Muslim, Abū Dawud, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah narrated from Abū Mūsā who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'When the imam recites' — meaning — '(not of those who have evoked anger, nor of those who are astray)', then say Amin, and God will love you."

al-Bukhari, Muslim, the authors of the Sunan, Aḥmad, Ibn Abi Shaybah and others narrated from Abū Hurayrah that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "When the imam says Amin, then say Amin, for whoever's Amin coincides with the Amin of the angels, his past sins will be forgiven."

Aḥmad, Ibn Majah and al-Bayhaqi narrated, with a chain that al-Suyuti called ṣaḥīḥ, from ʿĀʾishah that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The Jews have not envied you for anything as they have envied you for the salam and the amin."

Ibn ʿAdi narrated from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Indeed the Jews are a envious people; they have envied you for three things: spreading the salam, establishing the row, and Amin."

al-Ṭabarani in al-Awsat narrated the like of it from the hadith of Mu'adh.

Ibn Majah narrated with a weak chain from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: "The Jews have not envied you for anything as they have envied you for Amin, so increase your saying of Amin." Its weakness is that its chain includes Ṭalḥah ibn ʿAmr, who is weak.

al-Daylami narrated from Anas who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites 'In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful,' then recites the Opening of the Book, then says Amin, no angel close to God in the heaven remains without asking forgiveness for him."

Abū Dawud narrated from Bilal who said: "O Messenger of God, do not precede me with Amin." The meaning of Amin: "Respond (istajib)."

al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir: the meaning of Amin according to most scholars is: "O God, answer us," placed in the position of supplication.

He said in al-Ṣiḥāḥ: the meaning of Amin is likewise: "So let it be."

Juwaybir narrated in his tafsir from al-Ḍaḥḥāk, from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: "I said, O Messenger of God, what is the meaning of Amin? He said: 'My Lord, do it.'"

al-Kalbi narrated from Abū Ṣāliḥ from Ibn ʿAbbas the like of it.

Wakī' and Ibn Abi Shaybah in al-Muṣannaf narrated from Hilal ibn Yasaf and Mujahid who both said: "Amin" is one of the names of God.

Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated the like of it from Ḥakīm ibn Jubayr.

al-Tirmidhi said: its meaning is, "Do not disappoint our hope."

In it there are two dialects: the lengthened form on the pattern of fā'īl like Yasin, and the shortened form on the pattern of Yamin. The poet said in the lengthened form:

"O Lord, do not deprive me of her love ever, and may God have mercy on a servant who says Amina."

Another said: "Amin, amin, I am not content with one until I convey it to two thousand: Amina."

al-Jawhari said: doubling the mīm is an error.

It is narrated from al-Ḥasan, Ja'far al-Ṣādiq and al-Ḥusayn ibn Faḍl the doubling (of the mīm), from amma when one intends, i.e., "we are intending toward You." al-Qurtubi transmitted that.

al-Jawhari said: It is indeclinable, built on fatḥah like ayna and kayfa, because of the meeting of two unvocalised letters. From it one says: amman fulān ta'mīnan (so-and-so said amin).

The people of knowledge differed concerning saying it aloud, and whether the imam says it or not; this is explained in its proper places.
